message:
[OPENER — permission-based]
"Hi Gerald, this is Marisol Duarte with Ledgerline. I'm calling out of the blue, so I'll be upfront: this is a sales call. Can I have thirty seconds to tell you why I picked up the phone for you specifically, and then you can tell me if it's worth another minute?"

[If yes — the reason]
"Thanks. I work mostly with food distributors in the 200-to-500-employee range, and the controllers I talk to keep describing the same week. Day three of close, someone is still matching vendor credits against short-shipped pallets, the rebate accruals from your suppliers are sitting in a spreadsheet that one person understands, and the intercompany entries between the warehouse entity and the trading entity don't tie until somebody stays late. I don't know if any of that is true at Harrow & Pike — is it close, or am I way off?"

[PAUSE. Let him answer fully. Do not fill silence.]

[If he names a pain — dig, don't pitch]
"When you say the rebate accruals are the slow part, what does that actually look like on day three? Who owns it, and what happens if they're out sick?"
"And roughly how many days is close running today versus where your CFO would like it?"

[If he says 'we're fine']
"That's fair, and honestly good to hear. Out of curiosity, how many business days does close take you right now? ... Six is solid for a multi-entity distributor. The ones I talk to who switched usually weren't broken; they just wanted the reconciliations to run themselves so the team could spend day two on analysis instead of tick-and-tie."

[Bridge — only after pain is confirmed]
"What Ledgerline does is match bank, vendor, and intercompany activity continuously during the month, so by the time you hit period end most of the reconciliations are already done and flagged exceptions are the only thing left. A distributor about your size in the Midwest went from seven days to four in their second quarter on it."

[Ask]
"I'm not going to try to demo it to you on a cold call. Would it be unreasonable to put twenty minutes on the calendar next week where you walk me through your close checklist and I tell you honestly which pieces we'd help with and which we wouldn't?"

[If he hesitates]
"How about Tuesday or Thursday afternoon — and if after ten minutes it's not relevant, you have my permission to hang up."
buyer_reply: Yeah, look — the rebate stuff is real. We've got one senior accountant, Dana, who basically owns all the supplier programs and if she's on vacation we just push it to next month. Close is about seven days. I'm not looking to buy anything this quarter, but Thursday at two is fine if you keep it to twenty minutes.
quality_notes: Opens with honest permission, leads with industry-specific pain hypotheses the buyer can confirm or reject, and asks open questions before pitching. The meeting ask is low-commitment and framed around the buyer's own process.

message: Hi Rosalind, Devin Okonkwo-Hale here from Shiftwell — number's 555-0142. Quick one. I was reading that BrightPath opened three new clinics this year, and every ops director I talk to in urgent care says the same thing after an expansion like that: the schedule becomes a group text. Somebody calls out at 6 a.m., the charge nurse is texting eight people, and by the time a shift is covered you've paid overtime to the one person who always says yes. Shiftwell lets your staff swap and pick up shifts from their phones inside rules you set, so you're not the backstop at dawn. I'll send you a two-line email with a short clip so you can see it without a call. Again, Devin at 555-0142. Have a good one.
quality_notes: Short, specific trigger event, paints a vivid and recognizable pain, and gives a low-friction next step instead of demanding a callback. Number is repeated at start and end.

message:
[GATEKEEPER — Executive Assistant answers]

"Good morning, this is Thaddeus Mbeki calling from Patchbay. May I ask who I'm speaking with?"

[She gives her name]

"Thank you, Corinne. I'm hoping to reach Mr. Halvorsen regarding the integration work between your policy administration system and the claims platform. Is he available?"

[If she asks what it's regarding]

"Certainly. Patchbay is an integration platform. We work with carriers who are connecting older policy systems to newer claims and billing tools. I had a few questions for Mr. Halvorsen about how his team is approaching that."

[If she says he doesn't take unsolicited calls]

"I understand completely, and I appreciate you protecting his time. Would you be the right person to help me understand whether this is even a priority? For example, do you know if the integration project is being handled by his office or by someone in IT operations?"

[If she redirects to someone else]

"That's very helpful, thank you. Could you tell me the best way to reach that person? And would it be all right if I mentioned that you pointed me their way?"

[If she offers to take a message]

"That would be great. Please let him know Thaddeus Mbeki from Patchbay called about connecting the policy and claims systems, and that I'll send a brief email this afternoon with a reference from another regional carrier. My number is 555-0187."

[Close]

"Thank you again, Corinne. I appreciate your help."
buyer_reply: He's actually not the one running that. The claims integration is under Mike Ferreira in enterprise architecture. I can give you his extension but I can't promise he'll pick up — he's in back-to-back steering meetings most of this month.
quality_notes: Polite and respectful of the gatekeeper, and the redirect question is useful. However, the reason for the call is vague and generic, and the script relies on assumptions about the integration project without any research or specific value hook for the CTO.

message:
[DISCOVERY OPENER — prospect accepted a 15-minute intro from a webinar sign-up]

"Brandon, thanks for making time. I'll keep this tight. My goal for fifteen minutes is to figure out whether your cloud bill is a real problem or just an annoying one, and if it's just annoying I'll tell you and we'll both get time back. Fair?"

[Agenda confirmed]

"You signed up for the session on cost spikes after usage events. What made you register — was there a specific bill that made somebody upset?"

[Listen for the trigger. Common: back-to-school traffic, a GPU experiment left running, a finance escalation.]

"Got it. So the September bill came in about forty percent over forecast and finance asked you to explain it. How long did it take your team to figure out where that money went?"

"And who did that work — was it an engineer, a platform person, someone in finance?"

[Quantify]

"Rough numbers are fine: what's monthly spend now, and what percent of it do you think you could explain line by line to your CFO today?"

"If I'm hearing you right, roughly $180K a month, and maybe half of that is clearly tagged to a team or product. The other half is shared infrastructure and leftover experiments."

[Tie to Clearstack — briefly]

"That's the exact gap we close. Clearstack allocates untagged spend to teams based on actual usage, flags anomalies within hours instead of at month-end, and gives each engineering lead a weekly number they own. The typical first-quarter result for a team your size is ten to twenty percent off the bill, mostly from idle resources nobody remembered."

[Qualify the decision]

"If this looked right, who besides you would need to weigh in — is that your CFO, a platform lead, both?"

[Next step]

"Here's what I'd suggest: give us read-only billing access for a week, we come back with an actual breakdown of your spend and a list of what we'd cut. No commitment. If the number's small, we stop there."
buyer_reply: Honestly that's useful. The September thing was a load-testing cluster someone forgot to tear down, and it took Priyanka two full days to find it. I'll need to check with security on read-only access but I don't see why not. Send me the doc on what permissions you need.
quality_notes: Direct and time-respecting, anchors on the buyer's actual trigger event, quantifies the problem in the buyer's numbers, qualifies the buying group, and offers a concrete, low-risk next step.

message: Hey Annika, it's Colby, Colby Fairweather from Quorum HQ, um, we spoke — or actually I think we emailed — a couple of weeks back about the board portal stuff. Just wanted to follow up and see if you had a chance to look at the deck I sent, or the one-pager, or, uh, actually I think I also sent a case study. Anyway, Quorum HQ is basically a board and investor reporting portal, it does board books, it does investor updates, it has e-signature, permissions, version control, there's an analytics piece too. I know biotech boards are pretty intense right now with the funding environment so I figured it might be top of mind. So yeah, just checking in, wanted to touch base and see where your head's at. Give me a call back whenever, my number is 555-0119, or 555-0191, sorry, it's 555-0119. Thanks, bye.
quality_notes: Rambling and unprepared: unsure of prior contact, lists features with no tie to her situation, offers no reason to call back, and fumbles the phone number. 'Just checking in' gives the buyer nothing.

message:
[OPENER — pattern interrupt]
"Hi Kwame, this is Rhiannon from Fieldnote. I'm going to make you a bet: somewhere in your company's shared drive there's a folder called something like 'Customer Interviews FINAL v2' that nobody has opened since the person who made it left. Am I close?"

[Usually gets a laugh or 'how did you know']

"Ha — every product team I talk to has that folder. I promise I'm not calling to judge it. Can I take forty seconds to tell you why I'm calling, and you tell me if it's relevant?"

[Value statement]
"Fieldnote is where product teams keep their customer research so it's actually findable. You drop in call recordings and notes, it pulls out the themes and quotes, and when a PM is writing a spec for, say, merchant payouts, they can search 'payout delays' and see every customer who's ever complained about it, with the clip. The point is that you stop re-learning the same thing every quarter."

[Discovery]
"Can I ask how research works at Tidewater today? Is there a dedicated researcher, or do PMs run their own interviews?"
"When a PM wants to know what merchants have said about something, where do they go first?"
"Has there been a moment recently where you found out a team built something that customers had already told you they didn't want?"

[If 'we use our wiki for that']
"Totally reasonable. The question I'd ask is whether anyone's searched it in the last month. If yes, you might not need us. If it's more of an archive than a tool, that's the gap we fill."

[Close]
"I don't want to over-promise on a cold call. Would you be open to twenty minutes with me and one of our solutions folks, where you bring one research question you're working on right now and we show you what it would look like in Fieldnote?"

[If yes, lock in time. If no, ask: 'Who on your team owns research ops? I'd love to send them a short note.']
quality_notes: The playful opener is specific enough to earn attention without being gimmicky, the value statement uses a concrete fintech example, and discovery questions surface real pain. The ask is tied to the buyer's own current work.

message:
[CONTEXT — second call. Samir previously said they'd 'just do SOC 2 with spreadsheets and a consultant.']

"Samir, thanks for picking up again. Last time you mentioned you were leaning toward doing SOC 2 with your consultant and a tracker spreadsheet. I'm not calling to talk you out of that. I wanted to understand what's driving it, because if it's the right call for you I'd rather tell you that than waste your time."

[Listen. Likely: budget, 'we're only 120 people', bad prior tool experience.]

"That makes sense. You're one person covering security for the whole company, and the last thing you want is another tool you have to babysit. Is that a fair read?"

[Acknowledge before reframing]

"I hear that a lot from security leads at your stage, and honestly a lot of them do get through a first Type I on spreadsheets. Where I've seen it break is the year after. The Type II window means you're collecting evidence continuously for six or twelve months — access reviews, offboarding tickets, change approvals — and the spreadsheet becomes a second job. Does your consultant do the evidence collection, or does that land on you?"

[Let him answer]

"Right, so they write the policies and do the readiness assessment, but screenshotting the quarterly access reviews is you."

[Reframe around his time, not features]

"The way I'd think about it isn't 'Vaultline versus your consultant.' Plenty of our customers keep their consultant. Vaultline connects to your identity provider, your cloud accounts, and your ticketing system and collects most of that evidence automatically, so your consultant spends their hours on judgment instead of chasing screenshots. For a single-person security team, the time back is usually the whole case."

[Address budget directly]

"On price, I know you said budget is tight. If it helps, I can put together a side-by-side of what the consultant hours look like with and without automated evidence collection. If the math doesn't work, I'll say so."

[Ask]
"Would that comparison be useful before your planning meeting next week?"
buyer_reply: Yeah, I'll be honest, the budget thing is real but the bigger issue is I got burned by a tool last year that took three months to set up. If you can show me realistic setup time for our stack — we're on one cloud provider, one IdP, and a ticketing system — and the consultant comparison, I'll bring it to the planning meeting. No promises.
quality_notes: Acknowledges the objection without arguing, uncovers the real concern (his time and Type II evidence burden), positions alongside the consultant rather than against them, and offers a concrete artifact for his internal meeting.

message: Felicity, Jordan Ekwueme from Pipewise, 555-0163. I've reached out a few times about forecast accuracy and haven't connected, so this will be my last voicemail. I know quarter-end is coming and the last thing you need is another vendor in your ear. If the forecast your reps submit on Monday is close to what actually closes, you probably don't need us. If it's not, and you're spending Thursday afternoons scrubbing the pipeline by hand, I'd still be glad to help. Either way, I'll leave it there. 555-0163. Thanks Felicity.
quality_notes: Respectful, short, and the conditional framing is a decent self-qualifier. It's somewhat generic, though — no reference to Keystone Parcel's situation or any trigger, so it reads like it could go to any VP Sales.

message:
[GATEKEEPER — main line, receptionist answers]

"Hi, good afternoon. This is Priscilla Nakamura. I'm hoping you can point me in the right direction — I'm not even sure who the right person is yet. Who handles getting new hires set up with laptops and accounts on their first day? Is that IT, HR, or a bit of both?"

[Receptionists often know exactly — they see new hires arrive]

"Oh, that's interesting, so it's split. Does the new person usually have their laptop ready when they walk in, or is that a bit of a scramble?"

[If they share: 'sometimes they sit in the lobby for an hour while IT finishes']

"Ha, I hear that a lot. You probably see it firsthand. Who on the IT side handles that — is there a director or a manager?"

[Get name: e.g., 'That would be Lorraine Pfeiffer, our IT director.']

"Thank you so much. And on the people side, who leads HR?"

[Get name: e.g., 'Tobias Grünewald, he's Head of People.']

"That's really helpful. Would you be able to connect me to Lorraine? If she's busy, voicemail is totally fine."

[If asked 'what is this regarding?']

"Of course. I'm with Onramp — we help firms like yours get new hires fully set up before day one, so the laptop, the design software licenses, building access, and the HR paperwork are all ready when they walk in. Given what you said about people waiting in the lobby, I thought Lorraine might want to hear how other architecture firms have handled it."

[If transferred to voicemail — leave brief message referencing the lobby wait, and mention you spoke with reception]

"Thank you, Hector. You've been really helpful. Have a great rest of your day."
buyer_reply: Sure, I can try her line. Honestly, you're right about the lobby thing — we had two people sit here till almost eleven on Monday because their CAD licenses weren't assigned. Hold on, I'll put you through.
quality_notes: Treats the receptionist as an ally and source of insight rather than an obstacle, gathers names across both IT and HR, and uses a firsthand observation to make the eventual pitch concrete and credible.

message:
"Hi, is this Mei-Ling? Great, Brock Hennessy here from Tallyhouse, how are you doing today? Awesome. So the reason I'm calling is that Tallyhouse is the leading procurement and vendor spend management platform and I wanted to tell you about some of the amazing things we can do for Saltmarsh.

So first off, we have intake-to-procure workflows, which means any employee can submit a purchase request and it routes automatically. We also have a vendor onboarding portal, a contract repository with renewal alerts, three-way matching, budget tracking by department, a supplier risk module, spend analytics dashboards with over forty prebuilt reports, punch-out catalogs, and an AI assistant that can answer questions about your spend in plain English. We integrate with all the major ERPs and we have SSO.

And the reason I'm calling today specifically is that we are running an end-of-quarter promotion where if you sign before the thirtieth you get twenty percent off the first year and we waive implementation, which is normally a pretty big fee. This is honestly the best pricing we've offered all year and I can't guarantee it'll be around after this month.

Companies that use Tallyhouse save an average of eleven percent on vendor spend. For a hotel group your size, that could be millions of dollars.

So what I'd love to do is get you on a demo this week, ideally tomorrow or Thursday, with our solutions engineer so we can walk you through the whole platform. Does tomorrow at ten or Thursday at two work better for you?"
buyer_reply: I'm sorry, I'm in the middle of something. We just went through a procurement system selection last spring and signed a three-year deal. Please take me off your list.
quality_notes: Classic feature dump with no discovery, a manufactured end-of-quarter deadline, an unsupported 'millions of dollars' claim, and an assumptive close before learning anything. Didn't research that they'd recently selected a tool.

message: Hi Darnell, it's Gabriela Ostrowski from Beacon CX — 555-0128. We talked back in March, and at the time you said health scoring had to wait until after your team reorg. I saw on your LinkedIn that you've brought in two new CS managers since then, so I'm guessing the dust is at least partly settled. No agenda here. I'm curious whether the problem you described, finding out about at-risk accounts from the renewal call instead of months before, is still keeping you up, or whether the new structure has solved it. If it's still there, I'd be happy to pick up where we left off. If not, I'd honestly love to hear what worked. 555-0128. Take care.
buyer_reply: Hey Gabriela, got your voicemail. Reorg is done, mostly. And no, it hasn't fixed it — we lost a mid-size account last month that nobody saw coming. Can you do a call next Wednesday? I want my two new managers on it.
quality_notes: Re-engages with continuity from the prior conversation, references a credible trigger (new hires), restates the buyer's own pain in his words, and gives a graceful out. Warm without being pushy.

message:
[POST-DEMO FOLLOW-UP CALL — demo was last Tuesday with Lucinda and two contract managers]

"Good afternoon, Lucinda. Thank you for taking the call. I wanted to follow up on last Tuesday's session and hear how it landed with you and the team."

[Open-ended — let her lead]

"Understood. So the clause library and the playbook-based redlining were the strongest pieces for your contract managers, and the question that came up afterwards was around how Draftkit handles your distributor agreements, which have a lot of country-specific terms."

"That's a fair concern. Our approach is that the playbook can branch by jurisdiction, so the fallback positions for, say, an EU distributor are different from a Latin American one. I can have our solutions consultant build a small example using two of your actual templates, if you're comfortable sharing redacted versions."

[Next — process]

"Could you walk me through what an evaluation looks like on your side from here? Who else needs to be involved?"

"So the General Counsel signs off, and IT security will need to review data residency. Is there a security questionnaire you typically use?"

[Timeline]

"And in terms of timing, you mentioned the distributor renewals cluster in the first quarter. Would you want something in place before then, or is that too aggressive?"

[Close]

"Then here's what I'll propose: I'll send the security documentation this week, we schedule the jurisdiction example for the week after, and we include your General Counsel for the last thirty minutes of that session. Does that sequencing work?"
buyer_reply: That broadly works. I'd add that our GC is skeptical of anything AI-driven in redlining after an incident at her prior company, so I'd prefer we not lead with that on the call with her. Send the security package to me and I'll route it.
quality_notes: Well-structured follow-up with good process questions, but the script is a bit rigid and skips confirming business impact or success criteria. It also didn't anticipate the GC's stance, which a stronger discovery would have surfaced.

message:
[OPENER — CEO, likely between meetings. Be fast.]
"Ravi, Simone Abernathy from Quorum HQ. You don't know me. I'll take forty-five seconds and you can hang up after. Deal?"

[Reason — tied to trigger]
"Congrats on the Series B. Every CEO I've talked to after a B round tells me the same thing about six weeks later: the board just got bigger, two of the new investors want monthly updates instead of quarterly, and the board pack is now a forty-slide deck that your CFO and your chief of staff rebuild from scratch every time. Is that already happening, or am I early?"

[If 'that's happening']
"Who's building it right now — is it your CFO, or is it you at eleven at night?"
"How many hours does one board pack take, end to end, if you add up everybody who touches it?"

[If 'we're fine']
"Good. Then I'll ask one thing: when an investor wants last quarter's deck and the cap table, where do they get it? ... If the answer is 'they email someone,' that's usually where things start to slip once you have six or seven board members and observers."

[Bridge — one breath]
"Quorum HQ gives your board and investors one place to get the board book, the monthly update, and the documents they're entitled to, with the numbers pulled from your finance stack instead of pasted into slides. The CEOs I work with mostly care about one thing: getting their chief of staff's week back before the board meeting."

[Ask]
"I'd rather show you than tell you. Can I get fifteen minutes with you or whoever owns board prep — sounds like that might be your chief of staff — sometime next week?"

[If he delegates]
"Perfect. What's her name, and is it okay if I tell her you suggested we talk? I'll keep it to fifteen minutes."

[Before hanging up]
"Thanks Ravi. Good luck with the first board meeting with the new seats."
quality_notes: Short and respectful of a CEO's time, uses a timely trigger (Series B), frames a hypothesis the CEO can confirm, and smoothly accepts delegation to the right owner while securing permission to name-drop.

message: Hi Oluwaseun, this is Trent Gallagher calling from Ledgerline again, this is my fourth or fifth time trying you so I really hope I catch you this time. I sent you a few emails and a LinkedIn request too, not sure if you saw them. I really need to get some time with you this week because we have a limited number of implementation slots left for Q1 and I don't want Ironwood to miss out. Ledgerline is the number one automated month-end close platform and we can reduce your close by up to seventy percent, automate all your reconciliations, handle multi-entity consolidations, intercompany eliminations, flux analysis, and we integrate with every ERP. Honestly every CFO I talk to says close takes too long so I know this is relevant for you. Please call me back as soon as you get this at 555-0176, or if you can just reply to one of my emails with a time that works, I'll make it happen. Again it's urgent because of the Q1 slots. Thanks so much, talk soon.
quality_notes: Pushy and self-focused: leads with how many times he's called, invents scarcity around implementation slots, dumps features, makes an unqualified 'up to seventy percent' claim, and offers nothing specific to a construction CFO.

message:
[DISCOVERY OPENER — Curtis took a scheduled intro after an SDR set it up]

"Curtis, appreciate the time. Our SDR mentioned you had some questions about peak season staffing, so I wanted to start there rather than run through slides. Is that okay?"

[Confirm]

"Great. Can you walk me through how scheduling works today across your buildings? Who builds the schedule, and how far out?"

[Listen. Typical: site managers build weekly in spreadsheets, temp agency fills gaps.]

"And when you get a surge — a retailer moves a promotion up a week, say — what happens on the floor?"

"So the site manager calls the agency, and the agency sends whoever they have, and sometimes those people haven't been trained on the RF guns yet."

"How much of your peak labor ends up being agency versus your own people?"

"Roughly thirty percent agency at peak. And I'd guess the agency premium is substantial."

[Light positioning]

"One of the things Shiftwell does is let you open shifts to your own part-timers and flex pool first, before going to the agency, with rules around overtime and certifications. Some 3PLs use it to build an internal flex pool that covers part of what the agency was covering."

[Qualify]

"Is reducing agency spend a goal for next year, or is the bigger issue reliability — people not showing up?"

"And if you did look at something like this, would it be a COO-level decision or would each general manager weigh in?"

[Next step]

"Would it make sense to bring in one of your GMs for a working session where we map one building's peak week?"
buyer_reply: It's both, honestly — agency cost and no-shows. But we've looked at scheduling tools twice and the GMs hated them because they couldn't override anything. I'm not against another look, but I'd need to see that GMs keep control. Let me think about which building.
quality_notes: Solid discovery questions grounded in 3PL realities, but the script moves to positioning before quantifying the agency premium and doesn't explore the past failed evaluations, which turned out to be the main concern.

message: Hi Fiona, Leopold with Patchbay, 555-0134. I work with a few regional grocers who are connecting their point-of-sale, their loyalty program, and the e-commerce side, and most of them tell me the integrations are held together by a couple of scheduled scripts that one person wrote years ago. Not sure if that's the case at Brookfield. Patchbay is an integration platform that replaces a lot of those scripts with something your team can actually monitor. If that sounds familiar I'd love fifteen minutes. If not, no worries at all. 555-0134. Thanks.
quality_notes: Reasonable industry-relevant hypothesis and a polite out, but the value is stated vaguely ('something your team can actually monitor') and there's no specific trigger or reason Brookfield was chosen.

message: Hi Marcus, Harriet Oyelaran from Clearstack, 555-0158. Tanvi Raghunathan suggested I reach out — she and I worked together when she ran platform at Copperline, and she mentioned you're building out a FinOps practice at Northlight and are currently doing showback by hand from the billing exports. She thought it'd be worth a conversation, not necessarily about buying anything, more about how other streaming companies are allocating CDN and transcoding costs to content teams, since that's apparently the debate you're in the middle of. If that's useful, I'm happy to share what I've seen. I'll also send a short email so you have my details. 555-0158. Thanks Marcus.
buyer_reply: Hi Harriet — Tanvi mentioned you might call. Yes, the transcoding allocation fight is exactly where I'm stuck. I can do 30 minutes Thursday afternoon. Happy to talk shop first and see if the product fits after.
quality_notes: Leads with a credible mutual connection and the buyer's specific in-progress problem, offers expertise before product, and lowers commitment. The referral context is detailed enough to be believable.

message: Hey Jolene, Benedikt from Fieldnote, 555-0171. We chatted for a minute at the booth at the research ops meetup last week — you were the one who said your team has about four hundred interview recordings and nobody can find anything older than three months. I wanted to follow up on that. We've got a pretty neat way to tag and search across recordings, and I think it could help with exactly that. Would love to grab some time to show you. Let me know. 555-0171.
quality_notes: Good callback to a specific detail from the event, which builds recall, but the value statement is thin ('pretty neat way to tag and search') and the ask is vague with no proposed time or low-effort alternative.

message:
[GATEKEEPER — CTO's EA]

"Hi, this is Damon, I'm returning a call for Anders. Is he around?"

[EA: 'Can I ask what this is regarding? I don't see anything on his calendar.']

"Yeah, it's about the SOC 2 stuff. He'll know what it's about. Can you just put me through?"

[EA: 'He's in meetings until four. Who are you with?']

"I'm with Vaultline. It's kind of time sensitive. We work with a lot of companies like yours on compliance automation. Honestly, he's going to want to hear this because your competitors are all getting SOC 2 certified and if Cargoline doesn't, you're going to start losing deals. So it'd be great if you could get me fifteen minutes on his calendar today or tomorrow."

[EA: 'I'll need you to send an email and I can pass it along.']

"Sure, but emails usually get lost. Can you just block fifteen minutes? I'll send the invite. What's his email, is it first name dot last name?"

[EA: 'Please send it to the general info address.']

"Okay. I'll try back around four then. Thanks."

[Later that day — calls back the main line at 4:05]

"Hi, it's Damon again from Vaultline. Is Anders out of his meetings yet? I really just need five minutes. If he's not available, can you tell me who else handles security or compliance there? Maybe someone in IT? I just want to make sure the right person hears about this before end of quarter."
buyer_reply: I'll pass it along, but just so you know, he doesn't take calls from vendors he hasn't scheduled with. And we completed our SOC 2 Type II in August.
quality_notes: Opens with a misleading 'returning a call' claim that destroys trust once exposed, uses fear-based competitor pressure, tries to bully the assistant into booking time, and failed to check that the company already holds SOC 2.

message:
[OPENER]
"Idris, it's Constance Ferreira-Holt with Pipewise. I know CROs get a dozen of these a week, so I'll be brief and specific. Do you have a minute, or should I call back at a better time?"

[Reason]
"I noticed Sentinel Arc moved to a two-motion model this year — the self-serve tier for mid-market and the enterprise team selling platform deals. Most CROs I talk to who make that shift tell me the forecast gets harder, not easier, because the two motions have totally different conversion patterns, and the roll-up blends them into one number nobody trusts. Is that something you're running into?"

[Listen carefully — this is the qualifier]

[If yes]
"When your board asks for the quarter number, how do you build it? Is it rep commit rolled up, a RevOps model, or your gut adjusted for both?"
"How far off were you last quarter, roughly, and which motion drove the miss?"
"What does your RevOps team spend the last week of the quarter doing?"

[Value — short]
"Pipewise forecasts each motion on its own historical patterns — deal velocity, stage conversion, engagement signals — and then rolls them up, so you can see that enterprise is tracking to ninety-two percent while self-serve is at a hundred and ten, instead of one blended number. CROs use it mainly for the board conversation and for knowing which deals to personally get involved in."

[If he pushes back: 'we have a forecasting module in our CRM']

message: Hey Noor, Garrett here with Onramp. Hope your week's going well. We're an employee onboarding and IT provisioning platform that helps companies make onboarding easier and more efficient. message:
[DISCOVERY OPENER — VP Sales accepted a 20-minute call after a LinkedIn exchange about long sales cycles]

"Bartholomew, thanks for jumping on. In your message you said your deals take nine to fourteen months and your forecast is basically 'whatever the utility's procurement office feels like this quarter.' I laughed, but I suspect it's not that funny when the board asks. Can we start there?"

[Listen]

"So you have about forty open opportunities, maybe eight that matter for the year, and each one has a pilot phase, a budget cycle, and a regulatory approval step. Which of those three is hardest to predict?"

"When a deal slips from Q3 to Q1 next year, how early do you usually find out? And who tells you — the rep, or the customer?"

"How are your reps capturing where a deal actually is in the utility's process? Is there a field for that, or is it in their notes?"

[Reflect the gap]

"What I'm hearing is that your stages describe your sales process, but the slips happen because of the customer's buying process, and nothing in your pipeline tracks that."

[Position — tailored]

"That's a gap Pipewise is good at with long-cycle deals. You can add milestones from the buyer's side — budget approved, pilot success criteria signed off, rate case filed — and the forecast weights deals by which of those have actually happened, not by the stage a rep picked. With eight deals that matter, it's less about statistical modeling and more about making the risks visible early."

[Honest qualifier]

"I'll say it plainly: with forty opportunities, you might not need us yet. If your VP Finance is mainly frustrated by slip timing, a disciplined milestone field in your CRM might get you seventy percent of the way."

[Ask]

quality_notes: Builds directly on the buyer's own words, isolates the real forecasting gap (buyer-side milestones), and honestly acknowledges that a small pipeline may not need the tool yet, which builds credibility and a natural path back.

message: Hi Hyacinth, Tiago Brennan-Silva from Shiftwell, 555-0124. message:
[Opening — buyer has just said: "Honestly, my team can build these connectors ourselves. We've done it before."]

That makes sense, and I'd guess your team could build them well. You've got strong engineers, and the order-sync service you described sounded solid. So I won't try to talk you out of building. Can I ask a few questions so we're both clear on what "build" means here?

And since then, how often has someone had to go back into it? Say a vendor changes their API version, a token rotation breaks, or a webhook payload adds a field. [Listen for maintenance pain. Most teams undercount this.]

Here's why I ask. You listed seven integrations on the roadmap for next year: the 3PL, two marketplaces, the returns platform, the tax engine, the ERP, and the loyalty tool. If each one is a few weeks to build and then a few days a quarter to maintain, that's real engineering capacity going to plumbing rather than the checkout work you mentioned you're behind on.

For you, I'd guess the order-sync logic stays in-house and the marketplace and tax connections are candidates for us.

[Pause. Let them react.]

One option: pick the integration you're least excited to build. We'll stand it up in a sandbox with your team in a two-week pilot. Then you'll have a real comparison point, our time against your estimate, instead of my claims.

message: Hi Hollis, Desmond from Vaultline. You told me last week there's no budget for compliance tooling until Q2, and I'm not calling to argue with that. message:
[Personalized video, roughly 2 minutes. Screen share of a Tallyhouse spend view with mock data in the background.]

message:
[Context: Owen said on the last call, "My store managers love their spreadsheet. If I force a new tool on them, I'll have a revolt."]

Owen, I've been thinking about what you said about the spreadsheet, and I don't think you're wrong. If your managers built something that works for them, that's worth respecting. So I'd like to understand what they love about it before I suggest anything.

[Ask:] When a manager tells you the spreadsheet works, what do they usually mean? Is it that they can see the whole week at once, that they can move people around quickly, or that it's simply familiar?

[Listen. Common answers: "they can see everything on one screen," "nobody has to log into anything."]

That's helpful. Here's what I'm hearing from your side, though, and correct me if I've got it wrong. The spreadsheet works for the manager making the schedule. It doesn't work so well for you at the regional level. You told me you can't see overtime across the 14 stores until payroll closes, and that shift swaps happen in group texts you never see.

So the question might not be "spreadsheet versus Shiftwell." It might be how to keep what managers like and still give you the visibility you're missing.

Two things that tend to help with adoption. First, the Shiftwell weekly grid deliberately looks like a spreadsheet. Managers can drag and drop, and we can import their current template so week one looks familiar. Second, we usually start with two or three volunteer stores, not a mandate. Managers at those stores become the ones who sell it to everyone else, or they tell us it doesn't work and you've lost very little.

[Pause.]

Is there a store manager you'd trust to give it an honest try? Ideally someone who's a bit skeptical, because if they like it, the others will listen.
quality_notes: Takes the change-management objection seriously, separates the manager's needs from the buyer's, and proposes a voluntary pilot that turns skeptics into champions.

message:
[Objection on prior call: "We've scripted most of our provisioning in-house. I don't see why we'd pay for it."]

Thank you for making time again, Hye-jin. Last week you mentioned your team has scripted most of the account provisioning, and I'd like to start there, because it's impressive work and I don't want to dismiss it.

Could you walk me through what happens on a new associate's first day? From the moment HR marks them as hired to the moment they can open a matter in the document system. [Listen and note each handoff.]

Thank you. If I've understood correctly, the scripts handle directory and email accounts well. The steps that remain manual are laptop imaging, practice-management licences, and the conflict-check system, which requires a ticket to the records team. And offboarding is handled separately, by a checklist.

[Confirm.]

Onramp is not intended to replace your scripts. It can call them. What it adds is orchestration across teams: HR triggers the workflow, IT, records and facilities each receive their task, and you can see in one place what is outstanding for each starter. On the offboarding side, it produces an audit trail of access removal, which I understand your compliance partner has asked about.

I'd suggest we map your current new-joiner process as it exists, scripts included, and identify where Onramp would and would not add value. If the answer is "very little," I would rather we both know that now.

Would next Wednesday suit for that mapping session, with someone from HR attending?

message: Hi Theo, it's Bianca from Shiftwell. I got your email saying the board froze all new software spend through June. message:
[Objection from intro call: "Our PE sponsor sends us their template. We just fill it in. Why would we need a portal?"]

[Ask:] When you fill in the sponsor template each month, where does the data come from? Is it one system, or are you pulling from the ERP, the payroll system, and a couple of plant-level spreadsheets?

[Listen. Expect: multiple sources, manual copy-paste.]

message:
[Objection on last call: "Our site managers will never use another app. They barely use email."]

Kwame, I want to come back to what you said about site managers. I believe you, and I think it's actually the most important thing you told me. So let's design around it.

Here's my question: today, when a site manager needs to rent a generator or order extra rebar, what do they actually do? [Listen. Likely answer: phone the supplier directly, or text the yard, then send a photo of the invoice later.]

Right. And the problem on your side is that you find out about that spend weeks later, when the invoice hits AP with no PO, and by then you can't negotiate or redirect to a preferred vendor.

message:
[Buyer said on the last call: "Our savings plans are already maxed out. We've squeezed everything out of the bill."]

Idris, I took your point about the savings plans seriously, so I checked something. You mentioned your commitment coverage is about 85%, which is excellent. Most teams your size sit around 60%. So I'll concede that you've done the commitment side better than most.

Here's where I'd still push, and tell me if this is wrong. Commitments make each hour of compute cheaper. They don't stop you from running hours you don't need. On the call you said the bidding cluster scales up for peak traffic, and that nobody's sure it scales back down cleanly overnight. You also said there are "a few" old staging environments nobody wants to delete.

[Ask:] Roughly how much of the bill would you guess goes to things nobody would miss if they disappeared tomorrow?

[Listen. Whatever number they give, write it down.]

Most teams guess 5%. When we actually measure, it usually comes out around 15 to 25%, mostly idle capacity and orphaned storage. On your bill, even the low end is meaningful.

So here's the proposal. Give Clearstack read-only access for two weeks. We'll produce a waste report for idle, orphaned, and over-provisioned resources only, no commitment advice since you've got that covered. If the number is less than your guess, I'll tell you not to buy.

message: Hey Nkechi, Jasper from Quorum. Totally understand that at 30 people with three investors, a board portal feels like overkill. You're probably right for now! Just wanted to mention we have a starter tier. Anyway, give me a shout if things change. Cheers.

message:
[Context: Clementine said, "Last time we did an audit it nearly broke my team. I'm not signing up for another tool that creates more work."]

Clementine, thanks for being honest about the last audit. It sounds like it was brutal, and I don't want to be the person who makes it worse. Can you tell me what took the most time? Was it gathering evidence, writing policies, or chasing people in other departments?

[Listen. Common answer: chasing people. Screenshots from engineering, access reviews from managers, HR proof of background checks.]

For access reviews, managers get a single task in their inbox with a one-click approve, instead of you sending a spreadsheet around.

[Pause.]

Would it help to talk to another IT lead at a staffing firm who went through this? I can set up a 20-minute call with someone who'll tell you what went wrong as well as what worked.

message:

message: Hi Thaddeus, Juno from Tallyhouse. You said on Monday that vendor onboarding is owned by finance, not purchasing. Got it, and thanks for telling me. message:
[Objection from intro call: "We don't have the budget this year. Integration projects get funded only when something breaks."]

Sergei, last time you said integration work only gets funded when something breaks. I appreciated the honesty, and I've seen that pattern at a lot of manufacturers. So I'm not going to ask you to find budget that doesn't exist. I'd like to understand what "breaks" looks like for you.

[Ask:] When was the last time an integration failed in a way leadership noticed? What happened?

[Listen. Likely story: the nightly ERP-to-MES sync failed, the plant ran on stale orders for a shift, someone rebuilt it by hand.]

How long did that take to fix, and who fixed it?

[Listen. Often one person, the only one who understands the script.]

message:
[90 seconds. Seller on camera, then a slide with three numbers.]

Celestine, short version. You told me last week: "We tried forecasting software two years ago and the reps gamed it."

Two things about that. First, you're right that any tool that grades reps on activity gets gamed. Reps log calls to make the numbers move. That's why Pipewise doesn't score on logged activity. It scores on things reps can't easily fake: email reply patterns from the buyer side, how many stakeholders are actually engaged, and whether close dates keep sliding.

Second, gaming usually happens when reps see the score as a stick. In the teams where it works, managers use it in pipeline review to ask better questions, not to rank people.

[Slide.] Here's what we'd measure in a 60-day pilot with two of your regional teams: commit accuracy against actual, the number of slipped deals flagged in advance, and how many forecast calls finish under 30 minutes.

If those numbers don't move, you'll have spent 60 days and no money. Reply "pilot" if you want the scope doc.
quality_notes: Directly addresses a past-failure objection by explaining why the mechanism differs, adds a management-practice insight, and defines pilot metrics up front.

message: Hey Agathe, Dashiell from Beacon CX. Saw your email that you're not the decision maker. No problem! Just wondering if you could let me know who is, or maybe forward my info along? Thanks a bunch, talk soon.

message:
[Objection from prior call: "Our churn is only 6%. Health scoring is a nice-to-have."]

Tobiah, I want to pick up where we left off. You said churn is around 6% and that health scoring feels like a nice-to-have. Six percent gross churn is genuinely good for security software, so I'm not going to tell you there's a fire.

Can I ask about the other side of the number, though? What's your net revenue retention, and how much of the expansion comes from accounts your CSMs actively worked versus accounts that just grew on their own?

[Listen. Many teams don't know the split. If they don't, that's the opening.]

Here's why I ask. When churn is already low, the bigger lever is usually expansion. Health scoring isn't only for spotting risk; the same signals tell you which accounts are getting heavy use of one module and are ready for a second. You mentioned your CSMs each carry around 70 accounts and mostly prioritize by renewal date. That means a healthy account with expansion potential might not get a proactive call for nine months.

So I'd reframe it. The question isn't whether Beacon reduces 6% churn. It's whether it helps your team find expansion earlier.

[Pause.]

I'd suggest a quick test. Send us twelve months of usage and contract data for your top 200 accounts. We'll run them through the expansion model and you can compare its list with the accounts that actually expanded. If the overlap is weak, health scoring really is a nice-to-have for you, and I'll say so.
quality_notes: Agrees that low churn weakens the risk pitch, then pivots to expansion with a diagnostic question and a backtest the buyer can judge objectively.

message: Good afternoon, Delia, this is Ambrose Teague from Ledgerline. Thank you for your email explaining that any software purchase over $25,000 must go through a formal RFP. I understand completely. If it would be useful, I can send the reconciliation requirements other universities have included in their RFPs, so your team has a reference point when drafting yours. You can reach me at 555-0183. Thank you.

message:
[Proposal walkthrough call, CFO + Controller. Goal: confirm the business case and surface any blockers before procurement.]

OPEN
'Thaddeus, thanks for making time. I know you blocked 30 minutes, and I'll keep us to 25. My goal is to walk through the proposal, make sure the numbers reflect your situation, and find out what could slow this down. Sound fair?'

RECAP THE PROBLEM (in their words)
'When we met with Yvette, the headline was that you've added 22 practices through acquisition this year, and each one closes on its own schedule. Consolidated close is at 16 days and the board wants it at 10 before you go to the lenders next fall. Is that still the right framing?'
[Pause. Let them correct. If the number changed, update the case live.]

THE CASE
'The proposal is built on three things Yvette's team measured, not on our benchmarks:
- 340 bank and card reconciliations per month, about 70% of which are straightforward matches we'd automate

message:
[Call script — negotiation call with Gideon Park, Chief of Staff, Halcyon Therapeutics]

message:

message:

If Kofi raises the CRM migration timeline: acknowledge it, offer our solutions engineer for a separate working session, and keep it off the commercial call.

message:

quality_notes: Turns a competing-quote discount demand into a scope comparison, anchors on the CISO's real pain (stale evidence), offers a multi-year trade and an honest downgrade path, and sets guardrails on how to talk about the competitor.

message:
[Negotiation call — Thaddeus Mwangi, VP Customer Success, Northstar Mobile. Also on: procurement director Elise Varner.]

Context: Northstar wants a 3-year enterprise agreement for 140 CSMs, but procurement has asked for (a) a 30% discount, (b) the right to reduce seats by up to 25% annually, and (c) Net 75 terms. We can live with (c). (a) and (b) together are not workable; one or the other is.

Opening:

Agreed item:
"Net 75 is fine. I'll confirm that in the order form today."

The hard part:
"The 30% discount and the 25% annual seat reduction are both reasonable asks on their own. Together, they mean we'd price for 140 seats and potentially be paid for 79 by year three. So I'd like to offer two packages and let you choose."

Package A, flexibility:
"List minus 15%, with the right to reduce seats by up to 20% at each anniversary. This fits if you expect the CS reorg to shrink the team."

Package B, price:
"List minus 28%, with seat count fixed at a minimum of 125 for the full term, and the right to add seats at the same rate."

Discovery question before they choose:
"Thaddeus, what's your honest view of headcount for CS over the next three years? If you're planning to grow with the 5G business customers, B is clearly better. If the team is likely to shrink, A protects you."

If Elise asks for both:
"I understand why you'd ask. I can't put both in front of our deal desk with a straight face. What I can add to either package is a free health-model tuning engagement with our data science team in year one."

Close:
"Which package would you like me to formalize?"

Rep note: Let Thaddeus answer the headcount question; it's information procurement may not have.
quality_notes: Concedes the easy item early, explains why the two hard asks compound, frames two clean packages, and uses a discovery question that brings the business owner's knowledge into a procurement-led negotiation.
