message: Hi Cedric, it's Florentina from Onramp. Quick thought rather than a sales call: I saw that your January associate class is 34 people, which is about double last year's. Your current plan covers provisioning for 20 concurrent onboardings, so you'd be queuing laptops and account setup for the second half. A temporary seasonal bump would cover it for just January and February. I'll send the details by email so you can look when it suits you. Thanks, Cedric.
quality_notes: Spots a concrete capacity problem from the customer's own hiring plan and offers a temporary, scoped fix without pressure.

message:
[Context: Lindenmoor uses Tallyhouse for central procurement. Departments still buy via p-cards with no visibility. Odalys mentioned in the QBR that audit flagged p-card spend.]

Good afternoon, Odalys. This is Caspian Rourke from Tallyhouse. Thank you for the time.

I'm following up on the audit finding you mentioned at our last review, about departmental card spending. I'd like to share what we've seen at two other universities and ask a few questions about how you're approaching it.

First, a question: roughly how much annual spend goes through departmental cards today, and do you have a sense of how much of it duplicates contracts you already have centrally?

[Listen. Many universities find 15 to 25 percent of card spend overlaps existing contracts.]

Thank you. That's consistent with what we've seen. At Calloway State, for example, about a fifth of card purchases were for items on existing contracts, mostly lab supplies and IT peripherals.

Our Card Spend module connects to your card issuer's feed and classifies each transaction against your contract catalog. Departments keep their cards, but you see the overlap and can redirect purchases. It also gives the auditors a monthly exception report.

Before I go further, who else would need to be involved? I expect the Controller's office and possibly Internal Audit.

[Listen and note names.]

In terms of investment, for an institution of Lindenmoor's size the module is approximately $38,000 annually. Given academic budget cycles, I'd propose a pilot with three departments in the spring term, so you have data before the fiscal year planning in May.

Would it be appropriate to schedule a session with you and the Controller's office in January?
quality_notes: Well-structured and ties to a real audit finding, but the delivery is stiff and it moves to pricing before confirming the problem size.

message:
[Context: Crestline's admin usage dropped 70% since Bartholomew's site managers started building schedules in a spreadsheet again. Renewal is in four months. Previous CSM left in August with no handoff.]

[Open]
Hi Bartholomew, this is Ottoline from Shiftwell. I took over your account a few weeks ago, and I'll be honest, I'm calling because something looks off and I'd rather ask than guess.

[State what you see]
Since about August, most of your site managers stopped publishing schedules in Shiftwell. Only the Reno site is still active. Your hourly staff are still clocking in through the app, so it looks like schedules are being built somewhere else and entered later. Is that right?

[Listen. Don't defend. Take notes on the specific frustrations.]

[Likely responses and how to handle them]
If he says the auto-scheduler doesn't account for forklift certifications: That's a fair complaint, and it's fixable. Certifications can be added as a skill requirement on each shift. It wasn't set up during implementation. I can have that configured for one site this week and you can see whether the schedules it builds are usable.

If he says peak season changed everything: Understood. Peak brings a lot of temporary workers through agencies, and if they aren't loaded into Shiftwell, the managers can't schedule them. We have an agency import that a lot of 3PLs use. Would it help if I walked one site manager through it?

If he says the previous CSM never followed up: I'm sorry about that. It shouldn't have happened, and I can't undo it, but I can commit to a weekly 15-minute check-in through the end of peak, and you can cancel it anytime.

[Agree on a test]
What I'd suggest is one site, two weeks. We fix whatever is blocking them, and if the managers still prefer the spreadsheet, we'll talk openly about what that means for your renewal. Does that sound fair?

[Close]
Which site would be the best test? And who is the site manager I should work with?
buyer_reply: [Bartholomew, on the call:] It's the certifications, mostly. The scheduler kept putting uncertified people on reach trucks and the managers just gave up. Try it at Fontana. Ask for Rosalía.
quality_notes: Admits the account was neglected, asks before diagnosing, prepares for likely objections with concrete fixes, and proposes a small, reversible test.

message:
[Personalized video, ~2 minutes. Screen share of Pipewise forecast accuracy chart for Sentinel Arc.]

Hi Ezra, it's Orla from Pipewise. Your renewal is in February and I know you'll be in board prep in January, so here's a two-minute version of what I'd otherwise put in a deck.

[Show the accuracy chart]

This line is your forecast accuracy by quarter. When you onboarded, you were landing about 18% off your commit. The last two quarters you've been within 5%. Most of that improvement came from one change, which is that your managers started using deal-inspection notes instead of overriding the AI forecast with gut calls.

[Switch to the region view]

Here's the one place it hasn't worked. EMEA is still 14% off, and it's because about a third of their pipeline is channel deals that come in through partners and aren't in your CRM until late stage. Pipewise can't forecast what it can't see.

[Back to camera]

So for renewal, my recommendation is to keep everything as is and fix EMEA. We have a partner pipeline connector that pulls registered deals in at the registration stage. It's included in your tier, it just needs your partner team to set it up. I can run that project with them in January.

If you want to talk about anything bigger, like adding your customer success team for expansion forecasting, we can. But I'd rather get EMEA right first. Let me know if a short call before your board meeting would be useful.
quality_notes: Respects the executive's time, shows measurable progress, isolates the one area that underperformed, and recommends fixing it before upselling.

message:
[Context: Riverbend's renewal is in 8 weeks. They're on a 3-year contract ending now. The champion, procurement lead Daria, left in September. Thelonius is the economic buyer and has never logged into Tallyhouse.]

[Open]
Hi Thelonius, Anouk from Tallyhouse. Thanks for taking this. I know you inherited us when Daria left, so I'll keep it practical: I want to give you a clear picture of what Riverbend gets from Tallyhouse so you can decide on the renewal with real information, not a sales pitch.

[Three numbers]
I'll share three numbers, and you can tell me if they match what your team sees.

One: about $41 million of annual spend now goes through approved POs in Tallyhouse. Before implementation, about half your indirect spend had no PO at all.

Two: your team negotiated 23 supplier contracts last year using the price benchmarking reports. Daria estimated about $780,000 in savings from that, mostly in packaging and ingredients.

Three: average PO approval time is 1.4 days, down from about a week.

[Pause. Ask:] Is that consistent with what you hear from the team?

[Listen. If he's skeptical about the savings figure, offer to walk his FP&A lead through the methodology.]

[Discovery]
With Daria gone, who's running procurement day to day now? And is there anything about how the team uses Tallyhouse that's frustrated you?

[Listen. Watch for: the new owner may want a different tool, or there may be a hiring freeze.]

[Renewal]
On terms, you're coming off a three-year contract with a launch discount. A new three-year term would be about 11% higher than today, which still sits below our current list price. A one-year term would be about 19% higher. I know that's a meaningful change, so I'd like to walk you and the new procurement owner through it together.

[Close]
Could we put 30 minutes on the calendar in the next two weeks with you and whoever has taken over from Daria?
quality_notes: Re-establishes value with a new economic buyer who never used the product, invites verification, and is upfront about the post-discount price step.

message: Hey Konrad, Bettina from Ledgerline. Just checking in, haven't heard from you in a while. Hope all is good. Give me a call back when you can. Thanks!
quality_notes: No reason for the call, no value, and nothing to prompt a callback from a busy finance leader.

message:
[Context: Freightmark uses Quorum HQ for board packs. Barnaby's Chief of Staff, Elodie, told the CSM they spend about 40 hours a quarter assembling KPI slides by copying from finance and CRM exports. Quorum's Live Metrics add-on connects directly to those sources.]

[Open]
Hi Barnaby, Cosima from Quorum HQ. Thanks for giving me 15 minutes. Elodie mentioned something at our last check-in that I wanted to raise with you directly, since you're the one who sees the end result.

[Surface the pain]
She said assembling the KPI section of each board pack takes her team about a week every quarter, mostly copying numbers from finance and sales exports into slides, then double-checking them. Does that match your sense of it?

[Listen. CEOs often don't know how much time goes into this. If he's surprised, let that land.]

[Ask about consequences]
Has that ever caused problems? Numbers that changed between the draft and the meeting, or a director asking for something that wasn't in the pack?

[Listen. Common story: a late revenue adjustment means the deck and the financials disagree.]

[Introduce the option, briefly]
We have an add-on called Live Metrics. It pulls the KPIs directly from your accounting system and CRM into the board pack, so the numbers refresh automatically up to the day you publish. Directors can also click into a metric between meetings without emailing Elodie for an update.

[Be clear on cost and effort]
For Freightmark's plan it's an extra $9,600 a year. Setup is about two weeks and mostly on our side. The main thing we need from your team is someone in finance to confirm which numbers are the source of truth.

[Low-pressure close]
I don't need a decision today. What I'd suggest is we build a prototype of next quarter's KPI page using your real data, and you and Elodie decide after you've seen it. Would that be worth doing ahead of the March board meeting?

[If he hesitates on cost: compare to 160 hours a year of Elodie's team's time. Don't calculate it for him unless he asks.]
quality_notes: Brings an operational pain to the executive who may not know about it, asks about consequences before pitching, and offers a prototype on real data.

message: Good afternoon Emmett, this is Ludovica Ferrante from Draftkit. I'm calling regarding your renewal on February 1. I'd like to confirm whether your team still needs the twelve business-user seats added for the land lease project, since that project wrapped in October. If not, we can reduce them at renewal. I'll follow up by email with the details. My direct line is 312-555-0147. Thank you.
quality_notes: Brief, specific, and proactively raises a seat reduction tied to a known project ending.

message:
[Context: Medivault's VP Eng hasn't attended a check-in in 7 months. Clearstack recommendations are piling up unactioned (backlog: $340k in estimated annual savings). Renewal is in 5 months. Risk: they see Clearstack as a dashboard nobody acts on.]

[Open]
Radomir, it's Jonquil from Clearstack. I'll be quick. I'm calling because there's $340,000 a year sitting in your Clearstack recommendations that nobody has acted on, and I don't think that's a tooling problem. I think it's an ownership problem, and I want to help fix it.

[Pause. Let him react.]

[Diagnose]
When you bought Clearstack, Pavel on your platform team was working the recommendations every week. Since he moved to the data platform project in April, I don't see anyone actioning them. Is there someone who owns cloud cost now, or did it fall between teams?

[Listen.]

[If no owner]
That's really common. Here are two options, and neither involves buying anything. First: we route recommendations straight into your engineering tickets, assigned to the team that owns each resource, so it's part of their normal work instead of a separate dashboard. Second: I run a monthly 30-minute triage with one of your engineers where we pick the top five and get them done.

[If he says the team has no capacity]
Understood. Then let's do just the top three. They're all unused storage snapshots and idle load balancers, which is about $120,000 of that total, and none of them require a code change. One engineer, one afternoon.

[Close]
Can you give me a name? I'll set up the ticket routing this week and we can check in after the first month to see what moved.
buyer_reply: [Radomir, on the call:] Fair hit. It did fall between teams. Talk to Yasmin, she runs SRE. And yes, do the ticket routing.
quality_notes: Opens with a hard number, frames the problem as ownership rather than blaming the customer, and asks for a name and a small action rather than a renewal commitment.

message:
[Personalized video, ~2 minutes. Screen share of a Tallyhouse spend cube filtered to St. Aldric's clinical supplies.]

Hi Fintan, Marguerite from Tallyhouse. At the October QBR you asked whether we could help on the clinical side, since Tallyhouse only covers your non-clinical spend today. I've spent some time on that question and wanted to show you what I found rather than describe it.

[Show the filtered view]

This is the slice of clinical spend that already flows through Tallyhouse by accident, mostly because some departments raise POs for clinical items through the general catalog. It's about $14 million a year, and you can see the same orthopedic implant from three suppliers here at prices that differ by up to 31%.

[Pause on the comparison]

That's a small sample. Your total clinical supply spend is roughly ten times that, and most of it runs through your GPO contracts and the materials management system, which we don't connect to today.

[Back to camera]

Our Clinical Spend module would connect to materials management and compare actual purchase prices against your GPO contract tiers. I want to be careful here: I don't know yet how clean your item master is, and that determines whether this works in three months or nine.

So my suggestion is a data assessment first. Our team spends two weeks with your materials management lead, and at the end you get a written view of the likely savings range and the effort required. It costs nothing. If the numbers aren't compelling, we stop there.

If you're open to it, reply with the name of whoever runs materials management and I'll coordinate.
quality_notes: Shows real evidence from the customer's data, is candid about uncertainty, and offers a free assessment instead of jumping to a contract.

message: Hi Lennox, Desislava at Shiftwell. Two quick things. Your renewal paperwork is ready, same terms as this year. And I noticed your holiday schedules for December aren't published yet, which is usually done by now at your sites. If something's blocking that, call me back and I'll help sort it out today. 503-555-0119. Thanks!
quality_notes: Pairs a routine renewal mention with an immediately useful operational flag, giving a real reason to call back.

message:
[Context: Paymeadow passed SOC 2 using Vaultline. In the QBR, Ravindra said their largest prospects now require vendor risk assessments of Paymeadow's own vendors (fourth-party risk). They currently track 120 vendors in a spreadsheet. Vaultline's Vendor Risk module is a fit.]

[Open]
Ravindra, Ysolde from Vaultline. You mentioned at the QBR that enterprise prospects keep asking how you assess your own vendors. I'd like to spend ten minutes on that. Is now still okay?

[Confirm the problem]
Last time you said you've got about 120 vendors in a spreadsheet, and your team sends security questionnaires by email. How many of those are actually current right now, meaning reviewed in the last 12 months?

[Listen. Likely answer: 'maybe half.']

And when a prospect's security team asks for evidence, how long does it take to put together?

[Listen. Note the number of hours or days.]

[Make the case briefly]
Our Vendor Risk module does three things. It sends and tracks questionnaires, it monitors vendors for breaches and certificate expiries between reviews, and it produces the vendor risk report your prospects are asking for in one click. It uses the same control framework you already have in Vaultline, so your auditors see one system.

[Price]
For 120 vendors, it's $22,000 a year. I'll be direct: that's more than the module costs most companies your size, because 120 is a lot of vendors. If you can tier them so only the critical ones get full reviews, we can price it on 40 critical vendors instead and it drops to about $11,000.

[Close]
Here's what I'd suggest. Send me the spreadsheet, and we'll tier it for you with a recommendation of which vendors are critical. That takes us a few days. Then you decide whether it's worth it. Fair?

[If he says not now: ask what deal is driving the urgency, and whether the next prospect review is before or after the end of Q1.]
buyer_reply: [Ravindra, on the call:] Probably 40% current, honestly. And it took my team three days last time. Send me the tiering approach and I'll get you the spreadsheet.
quality_notes: Confirms the problem with numbers from the buyer, prices transparently, and offers a cheaper tiered option before the buyer has to ask.

message:
[Context: Calderbrook renews in 10 weeks. Procurement has requested a vendor review. Usage is healthy but concentrated in the research team; product managers rarely log in.]

Good morning, Rutger. This is Philomena Akande from Fieldnote. Thank you for your time.

The purpose of today's call is to prepare for your renewal and the vendor review your procurement team has requested. I'd like to make sure you have what you need for that review and to understand any changes in your plans for next year.

First, I'll share a brief summary. Your research team has run 236 studies in Fieldnote this year, and the repository now holds about 1,900 tagged insights. Your researchers log in an average of four days a week.

Where adoption is lower is with product managers. About 15 percent of the product managers with access opened Fieldnote in the last quarter. Is that consistent with what you see, and is wider adoption a goal for next year?

[Listen.]

For the vendor review, I'll provide our security documentation, the updated data processing addendum, and a usage report. Is there anything specific procurement has asked for?

[Listen and note requirements.]

On pricing, your renewal is at the same rate as this year. If you'd like to discuss adding PM-focused training, we can include that at no additional cost.

May I follow up by email with the documentation and propose a time in two weeks to review any questions?
quality_notes: Thorough and well organized for a regulated buyer, but reads stiffly and surfaces the PM adoption gap without much of a plan to close it.

message:
[Opening]
Hi Callum, this is Imogen Raskin from Fieldnote. I know I'm calling out of the blue, so I'll be quick and you can tell me if it's a bad time.

[Wait for permission]

Thanks. Some context: about eight months ago we ran a short trial with Furrow, back when Maya Lindqvist was leading research. Maya's since moved on, and I saw you joined as Head of Product in September. I'm not calling to pick up where we left off; you probably have your own view on how research should work, and I'd rather hear it.

[Discovery]
Can I ask a couple of questions?

First: when your PMs want to know what farmers actually said about, say, the irrigation scheduling feature, where do they go today?

[Listen. Common answers: Slack search, a shared drive, "ask Priya."]

Second: when Maya was here, the team ran about a dozen grower interviews a month. Is that still happening, or did it slow down after she left?

[Listen. If it slowed down, probe gently.]

What usually happens when a research lead leaves is that the interviews are still there, in recordings and docs, but nobody can find them, so the knowledge leaves with the person. That was actually one of the things Maya flagged in the trial.

[Bridge]
Here's what I'd suggest, and feel free to say no. Your trial workspace is still archived on our side with about 40 tagged interviews in it. I can reactivate it for two weeks so you can see what's in there, even if you never buy anything. A lot of new product leaders find it's a decent way to get up to speed on the customer.

[If interested]
Great. I'll send a short email with the reactivation link and a 20-minute slot to walk through it. Does Thursday morning or Friday afternoon work better?

[If not interested]
Totally fair. Would it be okay if I sent you the export of those interviews anyway? They're your company's data, and I'd hate for them to just sit with us.

[Close]
Thanks for the time, Callum.
quality_notes: Handles a champion departure gracefully, uses discovery questions suited to a new leader, and offers concrete value (archived interviews) even if no deal happens.

message: Hi Priyanka, Theo Abernathy at Vaultline. Jonah Whitcombe at Lumen Ledger suggested I call. He said you're about to start your first SOC 2 Type II and that you two compared notes on it at the security roundtable last month. Jonah's team used us to get through theirs in about four months. No pitch on this message. If it'd help to hear what they did differently, call me back at 415-555-0172, or reply to the email I'm sending with Jonah copied. Thanks.
quality_notes: Leads with the referrer's name and a specific shared context, states the concrete outcome, and gives two easy ways to respond within a short voicemail.

message:
[Open on Jasper at his desk holding a mug that says "World's Okayest Forecaster"]

Hi Freya, Jasper from Beacon CX. Yes, the mug is real, my team gave it to me, and no, I'm not taking questions about it.

So, we last talked in June. You were about to head into renewal season and you told me, very kindly, that you didn't have room for a new tool until it was over. Fair.

[Hold up a sticky note that says "Q3 renewals: done?"]

By my count, that season should be wrapped up now. And I'm curious how it went. Specifically: how many of the accounts that churned were ones your team saw coming?

[Beat]

Because when we talked, you said something that stuck with me: that your CSMs usually knew an account was in trouble about two weeks after it was too late to do anything about it. That's the gap Beacon is built for. We pull product usage, support tickets, and survey data into a single health score so the warning shows up while there's still time to act.

[Turn laptop toward camera showing a simple health dashboard with fictional accounts]

This is what it looked like for a company about your size. The red ones are the accounts that would have been surprises.

I'm not asking for a full evaluation. I'd love 20 minutes to hear how renewals went and show you what Beacon would have flagged in hindsight if you'd been running it since June. If the answer is "we caught everything," then honestly, congratulations, and I'll go find someone who needs me more.

[Smile, raise mug]

Link to my calendar is below. Thanks, Freya.
quality_notes: Playful without being gimmicky, recalls the exact reason for the pause and a memorable buyer quote, and proposes a low-commitment hindsight analysis.

message:
Hi Jun, Felix Morrow from Onramp. Got two minutes?

[If yes]
Thanks. You started a trial with us in August, set up the Google Workspace and laptop provisioning connectors, and then it went quiet after the first week. I'm not calling to chase you. I'm calling because usually when a trial stalls at that point it's for one of three reasons: the connector setup was more work than expected, a bigger priority showed up, or the tool just didn't fit. Which was it for you?

[Listen]

[If setup friction]
That's on us. Our solutions engineer, Aria, can do the remaining setup with you in one 45-minute session. You'd see a full new-hire flow running end to end. Want me to book it?

[If priority shift]
Understood. When does your next hiring wave start? I'd rather reconnect two weeks before that than bug you now.

[If bad fit]
I appreciate the honesty. Can you tell me what was missing? It genuinely helps us, and I'll close out the trial so it's not sitting there.

[Close]
Thanks Jun. I'll send a short recap email either way.
quality_notes: Clear, respectful structure with branches for common stall reasons, but stays generic and doesn't use anything from the trial data to show Felix understands Stonefield's onboarding pain.

message:
[Opening]
Hi Dr. Park, this is Benedikt Sallow from Tallyhouse. Do you have a few minutes, or should I call back at a better time?

[If yes]
Thank you. I'll keep it brief. Westbrook looked at Tallyhouse about a year and a half ago, before you joined, when the procurement office was trying to get a handle on departmental purchasing. The project paused during the budget freeze. I saw you came in as CFO this summer, and given your background at the state university system, I suspect vendor spend is somewhere on your list.

[Discovery]
Can I ask how you're thinking about it?

Specifically, do you have a clear view today of what each department is spending with outside vendors, and how much of that goes through a contract versus a purchasing card?

[Listen]

One thing that came up in the original evaluation was that about 30 percent of departmental spend was going through p-cards with no PO, mostly software subscriptions and event services. The procurement team estimated a fair amount of duplication, like three departments paying separately for the same survey tool.

Does that match what you're seeing?

[Listen. If yes, continue. If no, ask what's changed.]

[Bridge]
What we typically do with a new CFO is run a spend analysis on the last 12 months of AP and card data. It takes about two weeks, it doesn't require you to buy anything, and it usually surfaces a handful of consolidation opportunities you can act on right away. Several schools have used it to build their case for the next budget cycle.

[Ask]
Would it make sense to set up 30 minutes with you and whoever owns procurement now to scope that?

[If hesitant]
Completely understand. Would it be useful if I sent a one-page summary of what the original evaluation found, so you have it as background?

[Close]
Thank you, Dr. Park. I'll follow up by email today.
quality_notes: Bridges a stalled deal to a new executive with relevant prior findings, asks good discovery questions, and offers a low-risk spend analysis tied to her budget cycle.

message: Hi Dominic, Harriet Quayle at Ledgerline. Saw the news that Orthavance acquired Kestrel Surgical. Congratulations. When we spoke last year you were closing in seven days with one entity. Integrating a second set of books usually adds a few days until the consolidation is automated. If that's on your radar, I'd like to show you how we handled it for another device company. My number is 312-555-0148. I'll send an email too.
quality_notes: Good trigger and a relevant problem statement, but the 'another device company' proof is vague and the voicemail could give a clearer reason to call back now.

message:
[Mateo on camera, casual setting]

Hey Bronwyn, it's Mateo from Shiftwell. Quick video because I think it's easier than another email.

First, thank you. Your managers at Saltgrass have been on Shiftwell for about eight months now, and the shift-swap approvals have gone from something your GMs complained about every week to something they mostly don't think about. That's a win and it's really your team's.

[Pause]

Here's why I'm recording this. When we talked last month you mentioned that your ownership group also runs the Tidewater Taproom locations, and that their scheduling is still done on paper at a few stores. I don't know the people over there, and I'd rather not cold call them out of nowhere.

Would you be open to introducing me to whoever runs ops or HR at Tidewater? Even a short email saying "this is the person who helped us with scheduling" would be plenty. If it's awkward because of internal politics, totally fine, just say so and I'll drop it.

Thanks, Bronwyn. Talk soon.
quality_notes: Specific and appreciative with a clearly scoped intro ask to a sister brand, but runs a bit long for what it's asking and doesn't offer to make the intro easy, such as drafting the email.

message:
[Opening]
Hi Lavinia, this is Kwabena Hollis from Pipewise. Desmond Rourke at Tollgate suggested I give you a call; I believe he sent you a note on Monday. Is now an okay time?

[If yes]
Great, thanks. Desmond mentioned you two used to work together and that you've recently been asked to own the forecast at Freightmark. He thought it might be worth comparing notes, since his team went through something similar last year.

[Context]
For what it's worth, the short version of Desmond's story: their forecast was rolled up from rep commits in a spreadsheet, it was off by 20 to 30 percent most quarters, and the CRO was losing trust in it with the board. They used Pipewise to build a model based on deal history and activity, and within two quarters they were landing within about 6 percent.

But I don't want to assume your situation is the same. Can I ask a few questions?

[Discovery]
How is the forecast built today, and who owns each piece of it?

[Listen]

When the forecast misses, what usually turns out to be the cause? Deals slipping, deals that were never real, or upside that nobody saw?

[Listen]

And what's driving the change now? Is this coming from the CRO, the board, or your own push?

[Listen]

[Bridge]
That's helpful. Based on what you've described, the part that resonates most from Desmond's experience is probably the slip-rate analysis. It sounds like you know deals are slipping but not which ones or why.

[Ask]
What I'd suggest is a 45-minute session where we connect to a copy of your CRM data and show you historical slip patterns. If it's useful, we can talk about what a pilot looks like. If not, you'll still have the analysis.

Would next week work? I could also bring Desmond in for 10 minutes if you'd like to hear it from him directly.

[Close]
Thanks, Lavinia. I'll send a calendar invite and copy Desmond on the follow-up.
quality_notes: Uses the referrer's story as context rather than a pitch, asks focused discovery questions, and ties the next step to what the buyer actually said.

message: Hi Celeste, it's Ulrich from Beacon CX, um, I hope you're doing well, I know it's been a while, I think we last talked maybe in the spring or early summer, and I know things were busy then and you mentioned you had a lot going on with the reorg and I totally understand that, those are always hard, anyway I just wanted to check in and see how things are going and whether you might have some time to reconnect at some point about Beacon, we've added a lot of new things, so, yeah, give me a call whenever, my number is, uh, 646-555-0193, thanks so much, bye.
quality_notes: Rambling, filler-heavy voicemail with no clear reason to call back, vague timing, and no specific value; the empathy comes across as unfocused rather than genuine.

message:
[Opening]
Hi Viktor, Esme Callaghan from Clearstack. We spoke back in April. Do you have three minutes?

[If yes]
Thanks. When we last talked, you decided to handle cost optimization in-house using your cloud provider's native tooling plus some scripts your team wrote. That was a sensible call. You had the people and the instinct to own it.

I'm calling for a specific reason. You launched Emberfall in October, and from what I read, player counts came in well above forecast. Congratulations. Launches like that usually do two things to a cloud bill: autoscaling groups that scale up and never quite come back down, and a pile of short-lived environments for hotfixes that nobody tears down.

[Question]
So I'm curious: how has the in-house approach held up through the launch?

[Listen]

[If "fine, we've got it handled"]
That's great to hear, and honestly not common. Out of curiosity, how much of your team's time is going into it each week? That's usually the hidden cost.

[Listen. If it's significant, continue to bridge. If not, close politely.]

[If "it's been rough" or "we haven't looked"]
That's what we hear from most studios post-launch. The native tools show you the spend, but they don't tell you who owns it or what's safe to turn off, and during a launch nobody has time to chase that down.

[Bridge]
Here's what I'd offer. We can connect to your billing data read-only, and within a day show you idle and orphaned resources by team, plus your commit coverage now that your usage baseline has shifted. message:

message:

message:
[Opening]

message:

message:

message: Good morning, Mr. Asante. This is Philomena Garvey with Draftkit. I understand you joined Altimere as General Counsel this autumn; congratulations. message:

message:

message: Hey Sabine, Rocco from Onramp here! Hope you're crushing it. message:

message:

message:

quality_notes: Shows real research (careers page, reposted roles), ties it to a plausible pain, uses one credible proof point, and makes a modest ask. Natural, unscripted feel.

message:

message:

message:

message:

message:

message:
[Context: Victor said on the last call that his team won't trust AI-generated redlines and he's worried about confidentiality.]

Victor, thanks for making time again. Last week you raised two concerns - whether your team can trust the redlines, and what happens to your documents - and I'd rather take them seriously than talk past them. Can I start with a question?

When you picture Draftkit getting something wrong, what's the scenario that worries you most?

[Listen. Likely answers: missing a non-standard indemnity, misreading a co-tenancy clause, silently accepting a counterparty change.]

On confidentiality: your documents are processed in a single-tenant environment, they're not used to train any shared model, and you control retention - most real-estate clients set 30 days. I'll send the data processing addendum today so your privacy counsel can read the actual language rather than take my word for it.

Pick five retail leases your team already negotiated - ideally ones with a tricky co-tenancy or exclusivity clause - and we'll run them through Draftkit blind. I can also drop the seat count from 25 to 15 - you mentioned only about a dozen people actually need logins, with investors on free viewer access - which brings the total down another chunk. [If she needs to think:] Of course. That offer doesn't expire this week - it's tied to the two-year term and seat count, not a deadline. I'll put it in writing today so you can lay it next to the other quote.

Gareth, Beatrix Holloway from Tallyhouse - we talked at the Campus Procurement Forum about grant-funded purchases.

You said the hardest part at Larkspur isn't the volume, it's that principal investigators buy lab equipment on grant funds, and procurement finds out after the fact whether the vendor met the grant's sourcing rules. Then someone in sponsored research has to unwind it at audit time.

[Screen share: an intake form with a 'Funding source' field]

Here's a quick look at how Riverside State handled that. When a researcher picks a grant as the funding source, the request automatically checks the grant's rules - for example, competitive quotes above a threshold, or approved vendor lists for federal awards. If something's missing, the requester is prompted before the PO exists, not after. Sponsored research approves in the same flow.

[Back to Beatrix]

Their audit findings on grant purchasing went from eleven to two in a year. I don't know if your rules are as complicated as theirs, but if you send me one grant's sourcing requirements, I'll configure this exact form against them and send you a link to try it. No demo, no call needed.
